newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian Business News - May 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian Business News - May 30.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

In the latest of a string of oil and gas discoveries off Australian shores, Shell Australia and Cultus Petroleum NL have confirmed the massive Cornea discovery could contain up to 2,665 million barrels of oil. Cultus shares rose on the back of the news the estimation, which sees Cornea with the potential to exceed the largest of Bass Strait oil finds. Page 1.

Coles Myer chief executive Dennis Eck warned yesterday that the recent lift in the company's share price may have come to an end as the retailer's various apparel operations were continuing to suffer from intense competitor. However, Eck added that most of the company's other divisions were running to budget. Page 39.

Australian Stock Exchange managing director Richard Humphry added to the campaign by the ASX against further regulation of companies over corporate governance when he dismissed calls for more regulation as rubbish. Humphry said regulation would have a negative effect on economic growth. Page 39.

The A$1.5 billion Retail Employees Superannuation Trust (REST) has become the first industry fund to establish an in-house funds management team in a move that has been feared by the funds management industry for years. REST plans to withdraw about A$300 million from a range of external managers. Page 39.

Australian Gas Light managing director Len Bleasel said yesterday AGL would consider taking an equity stake and operator role in the proposed Papua New Guinea to Australia gas pipeline. AGL has been encouraged by reports of the likelihood of backing by United States giant Chevron Corp. Page 40.

Visy Industries owner Richard Pratt says the company's profitability was adequate considering tough trading conditions. Pratt believes main competitor Amcor Ltd is facing tougher times in its overseas operations. Page 40.
THE AUSTRALIAN

As Japanese brewing group Asahi Breweries yesterday indicated it wants to sell its 14 percent stake of the Foster's Brewing Group, and BHP continues to grapple with divestment options for its 37 percent holding of Foster's, the way could be open for majority contol of Foster's to be taken over. Page 23.

In what has been described as an "ambush marketing" move against rival Ansett, Qantas has signed up 40 athletes, 30 of whom are Olympians, to appear in advertising and promotions leading up to 2000. As Qantas claims the ads are purely based on sport, official Olympic sponsor Ansett will not take any action over the campaign. Page 23.

Cultus Petroleum said yesterday that preliminary volumetric estimates of the Cornea field in the Browse Basin off the north-west of Western Australia, determined by joint-venture partner Shell Australia, indicated oil in place of between 617 milion and 2.67 billion barrels. Page 23.

Following news that government changes could see News Corp able to lift its share in Seven Network to 25 percent, shares in Seven rose almost three percent to A$5.35 yesterday. While to move may weaken the 24 percent controlling stake of Kerry Stokes, it will mean a big demand for Seven shares. Page 23.

BHP spokesman Robert Porter said yesterday BHP Petroleum is encouraged by the Bir Sif Fatima North-1 well in the Ghamedes Basin in the Sahara Desert in Algeria, which is looking like being an increasingly important test area for the company. The well is flowing at a rate of 5,570 barrels a day through a 11/16-inch choke. Page 24.

Federal Resources and Energy Minister Warwick Parer said yesterday the Senate is moving to scrap export controls on spot sales of liquefied natural gas, a move welcomed by partners in the A$15.67 billion North West Shelf gas project. The partners are now preparing for new multi-million contracts. Page 24.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Weaker than expected March quarter industry sales and warehouse inventories have hit government's hopes of lifting economic growth to four percent in 1997/98 and vindicate the Reserve Bank's decision last week to cut official interest rates. Economists now believe the RBA could drop rates further. Page 29.

Half-year to March profits for the big four banks indicate the ANZ Bank is the hottest stock, while Westpac is the least attractive. The Commonwealth Bank remains attractive because of its high yields, yet analysts are recommending investors look outside the banking sector. Page 29.

Explorers in the Gawler Craton in outback South Australia are bracing for a long winter and hoping investor confidence in the area can be fully restored. However, the explorers want to increase positive sentiment in the area without falling to the hype that saw Gawler-exposed shares rise to unprecedented levels six months ago. Page 29.

Seven Network's largest shareholder Kerry Stokes, and Fairfax newspaper group chairman Sir Laurence Street have hit out at government proposals to limit cross-media rule changes to Sydney and Melbourne and allow an increase foreign ownership. Stokes said the plan was "farcical", while Street said he believed the plan would weaken publications and decrease competition. Page 29.

Southcorp Holdings chief executive Graham Kraehe said yesterday he was confident strong performances in the company's wine and packaging divisions would assist in offsetting the weak outlook for its appliance and whitegoods operations in the 12 months to the end of June. Page 31.

Visa International has been criticised by several banks for its decision to fine them A$10,000 for failing to instal compatibility requirements on merchant terminals, which will be used to overcome the Year 2000 computer problem concerning the ability of computer programs to deal with the change of date from 1999 to 2000 without disturbing the functioning of the software. Page 31.
THE AGE

Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released yesterday show manufacturers' sales and business stockpiles dropped three percent in the March quarter, news that overshadowed positive trade figures. Economists are now downgrading estimates of growth for 1997, with ANZ Securities predicting economic growth would total just 0.75 percent in 1996/97, and 3.5 percent in 1997/98. Page B1.

While Crown Casino is tight-lipped on its revenue so far, members of the financial community believe booming crowds have led to spending higher than Crown management expected. However, the huge crowds have not helped the company's share price, which is still at around A$2.00 to A$2.10. Page B1.

Cultus Petroleum, the only listed partner in the Cornea oil discovery in the Browse basin of Western Australia, revealed yesterday that the 50 percent owner and operator of the joint venture, Shell Australia, predicts the field could contain between 617 million and 2.66 billion barrels of oil, sparking a new enthusiasm in the oil sector. Page B1.

Following a conciliatory speech this week by Industry Minister John Moore, Prime Minister John Howard said yesterday the government was unlikely to take up the recommendations of the Productivity Commission to accelerate tariff cuts for the car industry. Page B3.

It is understood that the proposed deal between Coca-Cola Amatil CCA.AX and San Miguel Corporation of the Philippines has been delayed, as the two sides have been unable to thrash out the details within the planned timetable, such as a seat on the CCA board for San Miguel. Page B3.

A survey of 130 blue-chip companies by accounting firm Price Waterhouse found corporate Australia is in favour of national privacy legislation to protect customers from unwanted intrusion. The Privacy Survey 1997 found two-thirds of companies cannot enviage privacy legislation causing financial problems. Page B3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
